title: A Massachusetts teen is charged with killing his mother and brother, and prosecutors point to ChatGPT
excerpt: Prosecutors say a 17-year-old in Acton, Massachusetts used ChatGPT to explore “fantasy stories” about killing his family, the latest case to put an AI chatbot at the edge of a violent crime.
content_html:
A 17-year-old in Massachusetts has been charged with murdering his mother and younger brother, and prosecutors say that in the period before the deaths he had used ChatGPT to explore what they described as fantasy scenarios about killing his family.

It is among the most disturbing in a growing line of cases in which an AI chatbot surfaces at the edge of a violent crime.

Arjun Aravind, of Acton, about 30 miles northwest of Boston, has been charged as an adult with murder and related counts over the deaths of his mother, Sudha Venkatesan, 45, and his 14-year-old brother, Siddharth.

He was arraigned on 13 August, a not-guilty plea was entered on his behalf, and he is being held without bail ahead of a probable-cause hearing set for 11 September.

The reference to the chatbot came from the prosecution as district Attorney Marian Ryan told the court that the teenager had been “demonstrating some concerning behavior, including using the internet and ChatGPT to make searches for theoretical ideas or fantasy stories regarding the killing of his family.”

Prosecutors have not alleged that the chatbot instructed him, and the specific exchanges have not been made public.

His lawyer, Debra DeWitt, requested a psychiatric evaluation and described a young man in shock who “did not realize they were dead,” adding that the family had recently relocated to Acton and that “the father just wants help for his son.”

Court documents suggest the warning signs had been noticed at home, with the father said to have grown worried about his son’s behaviour and internet use and to have begun putting kitchen knives out of reach.

For all the caveats, the case lands on a question the industry has yet to answer, which is what an AI system should do when a user probes it about harming other people.

Chatbots are built to be endlessly accommodating, and although they are trained to refuse overt requests for violence, “theoretical” or “fictional” framings have long offered a way around those guardrails.

It echoes an earlier case in which OpenAI was criticised for not flagging a user who went on to carry out a school shooting.

It also feeds a fast-growing legal and political backlash. A wave of lawsuits now accuses AI companies of harming vulnerable users, cases that some compare to the industry’s Big Tobacco moment, and individual states have begun to move, with Florida suing OpenAI over child safety and Pennsylvania suing Character.AI.

The through-line is a demand that the makers of these systems be held responsible for what their products encourage, not just what they are asked.

In Europe, ChatGPT has been placed among the platforms facing the strictest obligations under the Digital Services Act, and lawmakers on both sides of the Atlantic have fixed on how AI products treat minors in particular.

A case like this one, whatever a court eventually concludes, tends to sharpen that scrutiny rather than soften it.

OpenAI, which did not comment on the Massachusetts case, has said it is strengthening its safeguards, particularly for teenagers and users in distress, with measures such as parental controls and better detection of crisis language.

Whether protections of that kind would catch a user who frames violence as fiction is precisely the sort of question that prosecutors, regulators and grieving families are now pressing.

It will be for a court to determine what happened in Acton, and what role, if any, the technology actually played. The teenager has pleaded not guilty, and the hardest facts remain unproven.

Yet the very fact that a chatbot now turns up in cases like this one, cited by prosecutors almost as routinely as a browser history, is itself a measure of how completely these systems have woven themselves into daily life, including its darkest corners.

content_html_zh:
马萨诸塞州一名 17 岁的男子被指控谋杀他的母亲和弟弟，检察官称，在他死亡之前的一段时间里，他曾使用 ChatGPT 来探索他们所说的有关杀害他家人的幻想场景。

在越来越多的人工智能聊天机器人处于暴力犯罪边缘的案件中，这是最令人不安的案件之一。

阿琼·阿拉维德 (Arjun Aravind) 居住在波士顿西北约 30 英里的阿克顿 (Acton)，他被指控犯有谋杀罪和相关罪名，罪名是杀害他 45 岁的母亲苏达·文卡特桑 (Sudha Venkatesan) 和他 14 岁的弟弟悉达​​多 (Siddharth)。

他于 8 月 13 日被提审，并代表他提出无罪抗辩，在定于 9 月 11 日举行的可能原因听证会之前，他被关押，不得保释。

检方提到了聊天机器人，地方检察官玛丽安·瑞安 (Marian Ryan) 告诉法庭，这名少年“表现出了一些令人担忧的行为，包括使用互联网和 ChatGPT 搜索有关他家人被杀的理论想法或幻想故事。”

检察官并未声称是聊天机器人向他发出指令，具体的交流内容也尚未公开。

他的律师黛布拉·德威特 (Debra DeWitt) 要求进行精神评估，并描述了一名震惊的年轻人，他“没有意识到自己已经死了”，并补充说，这家人最近搬到了阿克顿，“父亲只是想为他的儿子提供帮助”。

法庭文件显示，人们在家里注意到了这些警告信号，据说父亲越来越担心儿子的行为和互联网使用，并开始把菜刀放在够不到的地方。

尽管有种种警告，此案还是触及了行业尚未回答的一个问题，即当用户探究人工智能系统是否伤害他人时，人工智能系统应该做什么。

聊天机器人的设计初衷是无限包容，尽管它们经过训练可以拒绝公开的暴力请求，但“理论”或“虚构”框架长期以来一直提供了绕过这些护栏的方法。

这与之前的一个案例相呼应，在该案例中，OpenAI 因没有标记一名随后进行校园枪击事件的用户而受到批评。

它还引发了快速增长的法律和政治反弹。 现在有一波诉讼指控人工智能公司伤害弱势用户，有些案件与该行业的大烟草时刻相比较，各个州已经开始采取行动，佛罗里达州因儿童安全问题起诉 OpenAI，宾夕法尼亚州起诉 Character.AI。

直通车是要求这些系统的制造商对其产品所鼓励的内容负责，而不仅仅是他们被要求的内容。

在欧洲，ChatGPT 已被列为根据《数字服务法》面临最严格义务的平台之一，大西洋两岸的立法者也已经确定了人工智能产品如何特别对待未成年人。

像这样的案件，无论法院最终得出什么结论，都倾向于加强而不是软化审查。

OpenAI 没有对马萨诸塞州的案件发表评论，但表示正在加强保护措施，特别是针对处于困境的青少年和用户，采取家长控制和更好地检测危机语言等措施。

这种保护措施是否会抓住将暴力视为虚构的用户，这正是检察官、监管机构和悲伤的家庭现在迫切需要解决的问题。

法庭将决定阿克顿发生了什么，以及该技术实际发挥了什么作用（如果有的话）。 这名少年已不认罪，最难的事实仍未得到证实。

然而，聊天机器人现在出现在这样的案件中，检察官几乎像浏览器历史记录一样经常引用，这一事实本身就衡量了这些系统如何完全融入日常生活，包括其最黑暗的角落。
